system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2128-11-03 16:54:00 to 2128-11-07 20:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with brittle type 1 diabetes, recurrent gastroparesis, chronic kidney disease stage II, and a history of anxiety and depression was readmitted within 24 hours of discharge due to persistent abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting, consistent with a gastroparesis flare. Her symptoms were exacerbated by uncontrolled diabetes and possible gastroesophageal reflux. Chest tightness was evaluated with a normal chest X-ray, ruling out acute cardiopulmonary causes. She was managed with IV fluids, insulin adjustment to her home NPH regimen, and anti-nausea medications while avoiding contraindicated drugs due to allergies. She gradually advanced to a soft diet, with improvement in symptoms and stable renal function. Omeprazole was continued for acid suppression. A coordinated discharge plan included follow-up with her primary care provider, mental health support, and ophthalmology for background diabetic retinopathy. She was discharged home in stable condition with instructions for ongoing diabetes and gastroparesis management.
problems: Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type I [juvenile type], uncontrolled
Diabetes with renal manifestations, type I [juvenile type], uncontrolled
Hypertensive chronic kidney disease, unspecified, with chronic kidney disease stage I through stage IV, or unspecified
Diabetes with ophthalmic manifestations, type I [juvenile type], uncontrolled
Nephritis and nephropathy, not specified as acute or chronic, in diseases classified elsewhere

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms. ___,

It was a pleasure taking care of you while you were at ___.

You were admitted because you were having severe abdominal pain 
with nausea and vomiting at home as well as very high blood 
sugars.  This is a problem that you have had many times and 
likely represents worsening of your gastroparesis (poor stomach 
emptying) from your diabetes.  As you know, many things can 
worsen your problems with gastric emptying including having high 
blood sugar as well as certain medications (narcotics, zofran). 
You were continued on Reglan (medication to help with stomach 
emptying) and given pain medications to help with your acute 
abdominal pain.  Your pain improved while you were admitted and 
you were able to start eating again without further vomiting.  
We had you get a gastric emptying study to evaluate your 
gastroparesis, and the results of this study are still pending 
and will need follow up. We had you avoid taking narcotics and 
other medications that interfere with the results of this study.

You also had high blood sugars, with at blood sugar of more than 
700 when you were admitted.  The diabetes team saw you and made 
adjustments to your insulin medication doses.  Your sugars 
improved but not as much as we would like. You wanted to be 
discharged with high blood sugars still because you wanted to 
take care of your son. You understood the risks of leaving the 
hospital with high blood sugars. We would like for you to be 
seen in the ___ Diabetes clinic so that they can adjust your 
insulin once you are at home.  The high sugar levels can also 
worsen your problems with abdominal pain and poor stomach 
emptying.

You continued your usual dialysis and medications for your 
kidney failure while you were in the hospital.  We checked a 
hormone called PTH (parathyroid) which becomes elevated when you 
have kidney failure, and because it was high we started you on 
Vitamin D with calcium.  You should continue this medication at 
home.
  
We spoke with your kidney doctor, ___ agreed with 
our plan to place a port for better intravenous access (to give 
medications by IVs and draw blood).  However, your port 
placement was delayed before your were discharged.  You will 
need to arrange to come in to the hospital to get the port 
placed at another time.

At the end of your stay here, your medical team felt that you 
should stay to improve your blood sugar control.  You felt that 
your abdominal pain had improved and that you no longer wanted 
to stay in the hospital.  We explained that your sugars were not 
well controlled and that it was our medical opinion that you 
were not ready to leave the hospital.  You expressed 
understanding of our medical advice, and wished to be 
discharged.  We have set up a follow up appointment for you to 
be seen at ___ tomorrow ___.

We wish you all the best,
Your ___ Team

Dear Ms. ___,

It was a pleasure taking care of you while you were at ___.

You were admitted because you were having severe abdominal pain 
with nausea and vomiting at home as well as very high blood 
sugars.  This is a problem that you have had many times and 
likely represents worsening of your gastroparesis (poor stomach

worsen your problems with gastric emptying including having high 
blood sugar as well as certain medications (narcotics, zofran). 
You were continued on Reglan (medication to help with stomach 
emptying) and given pain medications to help with your acute 
abdominal pain.  Your pain improved while you were admitted and

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi… I’ve had this awful stomach pain for two days. It’s in my upper belly, crampy and burning. I’ve been vomiting, and once it had a little blood in it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And have you been able to keep anything down—food or fluids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing. I can’t eat or drink without feeling sick. The pain goes into my back too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I see you have a history of gastroparesis and diabetes. Did anything seem to trigger this episode?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Maybe the hot weather last week? But honestly, I ran out of my Percocet and couldn’t refill it. The pain’s been worse without it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll help manage your pain. Your blood sugar was very high when you arrived—over 700. Were you taking your insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I stopped my sliding scale because I wasn’t eating. I was scared of going too low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense, but high sugars can actually make your stomach empty even slower. We’ll adjust your insulin to keep you safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I didn’t know that. So my pain might be worse because of the high sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. High blood sugar slows stomach emptying, and so can narcotics like Percocet. We’ll work on both.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I get that. But I need something for the pain. Tylenol doesn’t touch it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you Dilaudid, which is safe for you, and a lidocaine patch for your back. But we’ll avoid certain meds that can worsen your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. I just want to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows mild fluid in the lungs, but no pneumonia. Your belly X-ray looks non-obstructed, so no blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from my heart or kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly related to your blood pressure and kidney function. Your BP was high when you came in—154 over 95. We’ve restarted your usual meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I missed a few doses. I’ve been so sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay. We’re getting things back on track. Your labs show your kidney function is stable for now, though your creatinine is high at 7.0.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your nausea seems better. We’d like to do a gastric emptying study to check how your stomach is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. But I heard I can’t take my pain meds before it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right. We need you off narcotics, Zofran, and laxatives for about 48 hours so the test is accurate. You took one Percocet 16 hours ago, which is close enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared the pain will come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use Tylenol and the lidocaine patch. And we’ll monitor you closely. The test is important to guide your treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The gastric emptying study shows delayed emptying—62% of food still in your stomach after 4 hours. Normal is less than 10%.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s definitely gastroparesis again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And being on Reglan helps, but high sugars and narcotics can still slow it down. We’re keeping you on Reglan and adjusting your insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been trying to eat small meals, but I just feel full so fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. We’ll keep you on soft foods and encourage small, frequent meals when you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re scheduled for dialysis today. We delayed it yesterday to do the stomach test.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. I know it’s part of the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugars are still high—around 400. The diabetes team increased your nighttime Lantus from 10 to 14 units.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’m not eating much. Won’t that make me low at night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re balancing it. Basal insulin keeps your baseline sugar down, even when you’re not eating. We’ll monitor and adjust at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want to go home. My son needs me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But we’re concerned your sugars aren’t stable yet. We’d like you to stay a bit longer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, but I feel better. The pain’s gone, and I’m not vomiting. I’ll follow up with my doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll support your decision, but we want you to know it’s not ideal. We’re setting up a diabetes clinic visit for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll go, I promise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked your PTH—it’s high, which is common in kidney disease. We’re starting vitamin D to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why my bones hurt sometimes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can contribute. We’ll keep an eye on it. Also, your port placement was delayed. You’ll need to schedule that as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I just want to get home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your exam looks good—vitals stable, belly soft. You’re tolerating food. We’re ready to discharge you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your meds, including the new vitamin D. Take your insulin as adjusted. Eat small, frequent meals. Avoid narcotics when possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Percocet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can take it as needed, but know it may slow your stomach. Use the lowest dose for the shortest time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I have my appointment tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, at the diabetes clinic. Call us if you vomit, can’t keep fluids down, or your sugars go over 500.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my sodium was low, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was 128, but that’s partly because your sugar was so high. We call that pseudohyponatremia. It should improve as your sugars come down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And your hemoglobin is stable, so your anemia isn’t worse. It’s related to your kidney disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m tired a lot, but I guess that’s normal for me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be. We’ll keep managing it. Rest when you get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last question—my anxiety’s been bad. Is it okay to keep taking lorazepam?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as prescribed—0.5 mg daily or for anxiety. But try relaxation techniques too. Social work can help with coping strategies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d like that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ll connect you before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel more ready to go home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad you’re feeling better. Take care of yourself and your son.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with type 1 diabetes, end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, and chronic gastroparesis was admitted for a flare of epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting, with a blood glucose over 700 mg/dL. She had stopped her sliding scale insulin due to poor intake and fear of hypoglycemia. Her pain improved with Dilaudid and lidocaine patch, and she was able to tolerate oral intake. A gastric emptying study confirmed delayed gastric emptying. Her insulin regimen was adjusted with an increase in nighttime Lantus to 14 units. Hypertension improved with restart of home medications. She developed pseudohyponatremia, which resolved with better glycemic control. PTH was elevated, prompting initiation of vitamin D. Despite ongoing hyperglycemia, she chose to be discharged home to care for her son, with a follow-up appointment scheduled in the diabetes clinic the next day. Port placement was deferred to outpatient setting.
